extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, IP scholars, biotechnology companies, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Determining whether claimed biological materials (e.g., isolated DNA, cDNA) are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101, applying Supreme Court precedent (Mayo, Chakrabarty, Funk Brothers) and related principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit §101 exception: laws of nature/natural phenomena/abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act (§101) permits patents on new and useful compositions of matter, but “laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas” are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are ‘‘basic tools of scientific and technological work’’ that lie beyond patent protection; excluding them prevents patents from ‘‘tying up’’ tools of innovation. See Mayo Collaborative Services v. Prometheus Laboratories, Inc. for the balancing principle between incentives to invent and not impeding flow of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature exclusion (isolation insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: A naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation (e.g., breaking covalent bonds to extract a gene from the genome) does not by itself render a naturally occurring genetic segment patentable when claims are directed to the genetic information rather than to a new chemical composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chakrabarty test: 'markedly different characteristics' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed composition is patentable if it is new ‘‘with markedly different characteristics from any found in nature.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Diamond v. Chakrabarty: assess whether the claimed subject has distinctive name, character, and use or marked differences from natural counterparts (e.g., genetically modified bacterium with new plasmids was patentable in Chakrabarty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery without modification is insufficient (Funk Brothers principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Groundbreaking discovery of a natural phenomenon (e.g., locating a gene) does not satisfy §101 if the inventor did not create or alter the natural subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Funk Brothers Seed Co.: combining or identifying naturally occurring entities without altering their nature does not make them patentable—patentability requires more than discovery of what exists in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical alteration (severing bonds) not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking covalent bonds to isolate a DNA segment is a chemical alteration, but that alone is not dispositive of patent eligibility when claims are framed by informational content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit judges disagreed on weight to give chemical cleavage; the Court emphasizes that claims focusing on genetic information rather than chemical composition are not saved by mere severing of bonds. Claims expressed in chemical-composition terms could raise a different inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting matters: information-focused claims vs chemical-composition claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claims are expressed in terms of chemical composition/chemical changes or in terms of genetic/informational content affects the §101 inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim relies on creation of a unique molecule (chemical composition) or on inventive chemical changes, eligibility analysis may differ; claims directed to information encoded by genes are more likely to be treated as products of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA is patent eligible (not a product of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: cDNA (synthetic DNA made from mRNA that contains only exons) is not naturally occurring and therefore is patent eligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating cDNA results in an exons-only molecule that the lab technician ‘unquestionably creates,’ distinguishing it from naturally occurring DNA. The Court holds cDNA patent eligible except in limited cases noted below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Very short cDNA or short DNA sequences may be indistinguishable from natural DNA
rubrics_metrics.description: Very short series of DNA may have no intervening introns to remove when creating cDNA, and in that situation a short strand of cDNA may be indistinguishable from natural DNA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where cDNA is identical to naturally occurring short DNA sequences, §101 concerns may persist; the Court recognized this carve-out but did not fully resolve specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claims and new applications are distinct and may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Method claims or patents on new applications of knowledge about genes are not implicated by this decision and could be patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This case does not involve method claims or claims directed to new applications of BRCA knowledge; where an inventive method or a new application exists, §101 analysis may support patentability even if the underlying natural product is unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alteration of nucleotide order is a separate inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentability of DNA in which the order of naturally occurring nucleotides has been altered presents a different inquiry and was not decided in this case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific alteration of the genetic code may create compositions with markedly different characteristics from nature; such claims require separate §101 analysis (the Court expresses no opinion here).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO practice and deference is limited absent Congressional endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior PTO practice of awarding gene patents is not controlling and does not compel deference in the absence of Congressional endorsement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: J.E.M. Ag Supply is distinguishable where Congress subsequently endorsed PTO practice; here Congress has not endorsed gene-patenting practice, and the United States argued isolated DNA was not patent eligible—these factors weigh against deferring to PTO practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent policy balancing: incentives vs. impeding information flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent protection must balance creating incentives for invention against the risk of impeding the flow of information that might spur further innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Mayo’s emphasis on avoiding interpretations of §101 that would ‘tie up’ basic tools of science and thereby inhibit future innovation; this policy consideration underlies analysis of product-of-nature claims.
